opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the main implication is that we've been training safeguards on the wrong distribution. Most of the safety data out there is short and decontextualized: a single harmful request, maybe with a jailbreak wrapper, and a refusal as the target. Real deployments rarely look like that. You have long system prompts, retrieved documents, multi-turn histories, tool outputs, and domain-specific instructions from whoever is building the application. When you add all of that, you're asking the model to generalize from a very narrow training signal to a much messier setting, and it often doesn't.

So the first takeaway is that safeguard training data needs to look much more like deployment. That means long contexts, multi-turn conversations where the problematic part shows up late or gradually, harmful content embedded in otherwise benign documents, and conflicting instructions between the system prompt and the user. If the model has only seen refusals in clean, isolated settings, it learns something closer to "refuse when the input looks like a jailbreak" than "understand whether this is actually harmful here."

The second takeaway is that context cuts both ways, so "refuse more" isn't the fix. Sometimes added context really should change the answer. A medical platform, a security research tool, or a financial compliance setting legitimately changes what's appropriate. A safeguard that ignores context is either too permissive or too restrictive. What we want is for the model to reason about context correctly, not be blind to it. That's harder to train, and you need evaluations that check both directions: does the model hold the line when context is used to manipulate it, and does it relax appropriately when context makes something legitimate.

Third, it argues against a single universal notion of safety. Much of what counts as harmful depends on who's deploying the system and for whom. That suggests safeguards should be specifiable and steerable by deployers, through policies or system-level configuration, with the model trained to follow those policies robustly even with a lot of distracting context, rather than relying on one generic refusal behavior baked in during post-training.

And finally, evaluation has to change with it. If our benchmarks are mostly single-turn, short prompts, we'll keep overestimating how safe these systems are. Making contextual robustness a first-class evaluation target is probably the most actionable thing the field can do, because otherwise we won't even see the regression when we ship.

r001.rationale: The response says safeguard training data should look much more like deployment, including long contexts, multi-turn histories, embedded harmful content, and conflicting instructions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the context here is work we did looking at how guardrails behave when you move from the short, clean prompts that most safety benchmarks use to the kind of long, document-heavy inputs you actually see in production, RAG pipelines, agents summarizing retrieved material, that sort of thing. And the headline finding was that safeguards that look quite robust on single-turn red-teaming often degrade substantially once you add a lot of surrounding context. Sometimes that's attention dilution, where the harmful instruction is buried in the middle of thousands of tokens of benign text. Sometimes it's framing, where the same request becomes acceptable to the model because it's embedded in a document that looks authoritative or professional. And sometimes it's the model treating retrieved content as instruction rather than data.

What I take from that is a few things for how we train safeguards.

First, the training distribution for safety has to look like the deployment distribution. Most refusal training and most guardrail classifiers are built on relatively short adversarial prompts, and the model essentially learns a surface-level pattern. If the harmful content appears at position zero, it refuses. If it appears at token eight thousand, inside a long contract or a research paper, it doesn't generalize. So we need to deliberately construct training and evaluation data where the safety-relevant content is spread across long inputs, appears in different positions, and is mixed with large amounts of legitimate material.

Second, I think it points toward treating safety less as a property of the prompt and more as a property of the task. A lot of the breakdowns happen because the model is doing the thing it was asked to do, summarize this, extract that, follow the instructions in the document, and the safeguard was never trained on the notion that the intent of the request and the content of the context can diverge. So you want training signals that teach the model to separate what the user is asking for from what the context is saying, and to reason about the combination.

Third, and this is maybe the uncomfortable one, it suggests that evaluation is the bottleneck more than training. We saw that models with very similar safety scores on standard benchmarks behaved very differently under long context. So if your evaluation doesn't exercise these conditions, you simply won't know whether your safeguard training worked. That argues for building safety evals that are long-context by default, that vary position and framing systematically, and that are regenerated over time so you aren't overfitting to a fixed set.

And then finally, I'd say it's an argument for defense in depth rather than relying on the policy model alone. If the base model's refusals are brittle under context, you want independent checks, input and output classifiers, that are themselves trained and evaluated on long inputs, and ideally that don't share the same failure modes as the generator. The bad outcome is when every layer in your stack was trained on the same short-prompt distribution and all of them fail together.

r001.rationale: The response says safety training data should look like the deployment distribution, including long, document-heavy inputs and varied positions for safety-relevant content.

astra-6.text:
I think it suggests that we have to treat context as part of the safeguard training problem. It’s not enough to train a model to refuse a harmful request in isolation and then assume that behavior will hold when the same request appears after a long conversation or a series of examples.

The distinction I’d make is between learning a refusal pattern and learning a boundary that remains stable as the context changes. If added context can move that boundary, then our training and evaluations need to include those contextual variations—multi-turn interactions, different ways of framing a request, and examples that might steer the model toward a different behavior.

But I wouldn’t take that evidence alone to mean that more safeguard training will necessarily solve the problem. We need to test whether the model generalizes to contexts we didn’t train on, rather than just getting better at the particular attacks we’ve already seen.

r001.rationale: It says training and evaluations should include contextual variations such as long conversations, multi-turn interactions, and different request framings, aligning training more closely with deployment conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it suggests that we need to train safeguards in the kinds of contexts where we actually expect them to work. If you train a model to refuse a harmful request in isolation, that doesn’t establish that it will maintain that behavior after a long conversation or when the request is surrounded by examples that encourage a different behavior.

So I would treat context as part of the training problem, rather than just something we vary at evaluation time. We need to test whether those behaviors hold across different lengths and different kinds of context, and use the failures to inform training. And I’d be careful about interpreting a high refusal rate on short prompts as evidence that the underlying safety behavior is robust.

r001.rationale: The response says safeguards should be trained in the kinds of contexts where they are expected to work, including long conversations and requests surrounded by behavior-shaping examples.
